text: By late summer 1992, the cracks were showing.
John Major was now Prime Minister.
In August, his new Chancellor, Norman Lamont,
said Britain would do whatever is necessary to stay in.
On September 3rd, the government announced it would borrow 10 billion ECU,
Europe's accounting currency, about 7 billion pounds to defend Sterling.
Then Italy blinked.
Over the weekend of September 12, the lira was devalued by 7%. In return, Germany trimmed
its rates. Just slightly. Less than markets hoped.
Then came the spark. On Tuesday, September 15, after the London markets closed, Schlesinger
spoke to reporters from Hundelsblatt and the Wall Street Journal. In substance, the
weekend's deal should have been broader and more pressure on currencies couldn't
be ruled out. By that evening, it was on the news wires. Traders read it one way. The pound
is next. That day, the Bank of England had already sold about $788 million to prop up
the pound. It closed at 2.7812, barely above the floor.
Druckenmiller wanted to add to the bet. According to Druckenmiller himself and financial historian
Sebastian Malaby, Soros told him to go for the jugular. They didn't just bet
the fund, they bet roughly twice the fund. By Soros' own estimate, the position
was worth almost ten billion dollars. Ten billion? Against one country?
Against one promise, sweetheart. Before we get to Wednesday morning, every money
trick in this story worked because people didn't look closely. Looking
closely is the whole point of money mirage. If that's your thing, subscribe. Now, 8 a.m.
